analysis.one_liner: Ends the health insurance industry's special exemption from federal antitrust laws.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 406-19 on February 24, 2010, but the Senate never voted, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: For 65 years, health insurers have had a special exemption under a law called the McCarran-Ferguson Act that shields them from federal antitrust enforcement — the laws used to stop price-fixing, collusion, and monopolies. This bill removed that shield for health insurers, allowing the Justice Department, regulators, and consumers to sue insurers the same way other industries can be sued. The House passed it 406-19, but the Senate never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and small businesses buying health insurance. Removing the antitrust exemption would let federal enforcers and private plaintiffs challenge insurers colluding on prices or dividing up markets, with the aim of lowering premiums through more competition.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the McCarran-Ferguson Act so that federal antitrust laws apply fully to health insurers, exposing practices like price signaling and market division to antitrust suits.
It applies prohibitions on unfair methods of competition to health insurance regardless of whether the business is run for profit, closing a loophole for nonprofit plans.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, who would lose the special protection from federal antitrust suits that they have had since 1945, and could face lawsuits and breakup of market dominance.

drawbacks.text: Republican opponents offered a motion to recommit that would have required the bill to be amended to modify the McCarran-Ferguson Act more broadly and to add a GAO report; it failed 170-249, with 165 of 178 House Republicans voting for it [S7].

Critics argued the exemption for insurers was limited and that antitrust suits take years to lower prices, so the bill's practical premium impact might be small; the bill itself contains no rate regulation or direct price controls [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — antitrust enforcement against insurers — is real but modest on its own; industry consolidation was one of several drivers of rising premiums. The costs are small: insurers lose a 65-year-old exemption that nearly every other industry lacks. The bill's weakness was not design but follow-through: passing the House 406-19 meant little once the Senate let it sit.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it overwhelmingly on a 406-19 vote, but the Senate placed it on its calendar and never brought it to a vote, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced February 22, 2010, the bill was referred to the Judiciary Committee but brought straight to the floor under a rule and passed on February 24 by a vote of 406-19 [S6].
The Senate received the bill on February 25, 2010, and placed it on its legislative calendar, where it remained without ever reaching a vote before the 111th Congress ended [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers kept the antitrust exemption that shields them from federal antitrust suits. Consumers gained nothing from the House's 406-19 vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers, who kept their exemption

for.name: Thomas Perriello
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it passed the House with broad support.

for.name: 253 of 253 House Democrats and 153 of 178 House Republicans

against.name: 165 of 178 Senate-bound House Republicans
against.role: House Republicans voting on the motion to recommit
against.what_they_did: Voted for a motion to recommit that would have sent the bill back to committee with instructions to amend the McCarran-Ferguson Act more broadly and add a GAO report; it failed 170-249.

against.name: U.S. Senate
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, placed it on the legislative calendar under General Orders, and never brought it to a vote before the Congress ended [S6].

sides.party_line_note: Final passage was overwhelming and bipartisan (406-19, with 253 Democrats and 153 Republicans in favor), but the motion to recommit split sharply by party, 165 Republicans for and 246 Democrats against, and the bill still died in the Senate without a vote [S7][S8].

industries.note: The bill strips health insurers of their special antitrust exemption under the McCarran-Ferguson Act, exposing them to antitrust suits for collusion, price-fixing, and monopolization that other industries already face.
